title: Junction, what's your function? Mapping the exon junction complex in Arabidopsis
content: In most eukaryotic genes, the protein-coding exons are interrupted by introns. These introns are cut out of the precursor mRNA by the spliceosome, a large molecular machine that then stitches the flanking exons together. But intron splicing leaves behind more than just properly joined exons. At each exon–exon junction, the spliceosome deposits a protein assembly called the exon junction complex (EJC), creating a molecular mark that stays with the mRNAs throughout their life cycle. In animals, the EJC orchestrates several aspects of RNA metabolism, from nuclear export and translation to nonsense-mediated decay, the surveillance pathway that removes transcripts carrying premature stop codons (He and Jacobson 2015; Woodward et al. 2017). Whether plants use the EJC in a similar manner has remained an open question, largely because technical limitations have prevented genome-wide mapping of EJC deposition in vivo. In their latest study, Kaiwen Sun and colleagues overcome these challenges and provide the first high-resolution map of the Arabidopsis EJC, revealing that plants assemble the complex in a conserved yet functionally distinct manner (Sun et al. 2026).
